speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks, I wish to congratulate my two colleagues, the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery) and the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier), the mover and the seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. They dealt with very important matters on various levels.
Mr. Speaker, the criticism made following the reading of the Speech from the Throne was the same as always, too many generalities, too many omissions, etc.
The Speech from the Throne is a document that stresses the points on which the government intends to legislate during the present session, but some events like the energy crisis during the last session may require bringing other pieces of legislation before Parliament.
But usually, as the session goes on, the legislative program set forth in the Speech from the Throne is brought before Parliament, amended in certain cases and finally passed. The speech read by the Governor General on February 27 deals with several economic, social and scientific matters, such as the energy crisis, inflation, means designed to offset its consequences and ensure supplies to

March 5, 1974
The Address-Mr. Clermont
consumers at reasonable prices in the near and distant future.
So it is proposed to help small and medium-sized businesses, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Canada Pension Plan. First, I would like to deal with inflation which has spared no country in 1973. Several factors have caused the increase in prices, like bad crops, the growth of world population and, in many parts of the world, the shortage of food, changes in eating habits, the strong economic growth in several industrial countries like Canada, which actual growth rate was the highest in the last 17 years, have experienced in 1973 which has brought about a shortage of basic materials and food, the decrease of oil exports by some producing countries and price increases.
All these cases I just outlined have bad effects on food prices, materials and products involved in industrial processing and the building trade. In order to alleviate these effects, the federal government chose selective measures and continues to do so. Inflation strikes everybody, but particularly large families, people on average or fixed income as well as a large number of retired persons.
That is why we have seen the federal government pay subsidies to limit price increases of various items, such as bread, milk, heating oil, gasoline and other oil products, amend tariffs to allow greater imports of fruits and vegetables, increase old age pensions and the guaranted income supplement, increase family allowances gearing them to the cost of living. The sales tax on children's clothing has been removed and the personal income tax geared to the cost of living.
In the Speech from the Throne, the government announces its intention of taking steps to increase food production; I hope it will do the same with regard to industrial products and thus reduce the pressure on prices.
The official opposition prefers an overall price and salary freeze for a period of 90 days. It is not very clear about what steps would follow. Recently, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) suggested, also to counter inflation, doing away with the sales tax on building materials and clothing.
With regard to the tax on building materials, he did not specify what measures would make up the reduction in income that would amount to about $500 million. Some may say that government expenditures will be cut down; Mr. Speaker, that reminds me of the experience with the conservative government: from May 1957 to 1963 they made the same promise. What was the result? An annual increase in expenditures.
The progressive conservative party might perhaps want to increase personal income taxes to make up the' shortage. Who knows?
Mr. Speaker, we are aware of the experience of the United States and the United Kingdon in the area of price and wage controls which, following completion of Phase IV of the program, resulted in an exhaustion of supply sources and the spiralling of prices in the United States.
Here is what the policy of the Progressive Conservative Party was on inflation, as reported in the March 1, 1974

issue of the Montreal Gazette by Mr. John Meyer, the former financial critic with this newspaper, and I quote: [English.]
The Conservatives, predictably, have persisted in their argument for controls-surely an anomolous position for the party bearing the name it does to be in. They have been making that argument for so long, and with such indifference to the experience of other countries where controls have been used, that it has begun to threaten their credibility as an alternative to both the Liberals and the New Democrats.
Their persistence is curious in view of the number of senior members of the party with business and financial backgrounds, both practical and academic. There was, and still may be although with clearly reduced force, an argument for controls on strictly political grounds. Controls would be evidence of a government's determination to explore every means of containing inflation and some stability in prices might even be achieved over the short run.
But as the definition and scope of inflation has become clearer, and its source largely found to lie in the inability of production to keep abreast of demand, controls can now be seen more likely to prolong and intensify inflation than to contain it. That is what is happening in the U.S. where continuing shortages of both basic commodities and finished products are directly attributable to the inability of producers to adequately cover their costs.
Mr. Speaker, the labour and industrial sectors will not generally support a global policy of price controls, no matter their duration. Some quarters consider that the present state of inflation is attributable to the growth of spending by the various levels of government, and of the money supply. Under these circumstances, in view of the problems resulting from the energy crisis, I feel it would be a gross lack of responsibility to minimize them, since it may happen that because of the increase in the price of oil, which tripled within the past six months, some of our trading partners may face serious problems as far as their balance of payments is concerned. This could result in a very considerable decrease in their economic growth, and we are aware of the impact of our exports on our economy.
The results of a recent survey indicated that the biggest problem for many Canadians is that of energy. It will be recalled that in June 1973, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources published a paper on energy in Canada. Among other things, the study analyzed energy supply and demand in Canada and many measures that could be implemented. It was then proven that they were most timely, following what happened in the fall of 1973 when some producing countries cut back their crude oil exports and greatly increased prices. At that time, two major problems came up, that of supply and that of prices which Canadian consumers would have to pay.
As far as supplies are concerned, we know that Canada was divided in two ever since 1961 by a line known as the Ottawa Valley or Borden Line. West of this line, oil was mainly shipped from western Canada by pipeline. Consumers east of the line were supplied mainly by cheaper oil imported from a number of producing countries in the middle East and Venezuela. In this case, means of transportation had to be provided without delay in order to ensure a constant flow of oil in this part of the country.
On September 4 and December 6, 1973, the Prime Minister of Canada advised the House of the action the government would take to deal with this difficult situation. On September 4, 1973, he announced the following steps:

1.	The oil industry will be asked to refrain from making further price increases affecting Canadian consumers before January 30, 1974. This price restraint would apply except where, to the satisfaction of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), the increase in the cost of imported crude oil warrants a Canadian price increase.
2.	The government intends to seek a control mechanism whereby higher prices in the U.S. market would not automatically increase prices at home in Canada.
3.	The government will also hold early consultations with provinces and industry on the extension of pipeline facilities so as to enable Canadian oil to be shipped into Montreal. At a time of rapidly escalating international prices, this would put Canadian oil into competition with international oil and would give additional security against international disruption of supply.
In the meantime, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, with the co-operation of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), was setting up additional means of transportation to provide adequate supplies to the residents of Quebec and the Atlantic provinces, either through the re-opening of the pipeline between Toronto and Ottawa which had been closed in 1962 or through the St. Lawrence Seaway from Sarnia to Montreal, until the closing of the latter, or by rail, truck or tanker from Vancouver to Montreal, the latter going through the Panama Canal. In December 1973, the Prime Minister announced further measures such as:
1.	The creation of a unique national market, the effect of which will be to abolish the "Borden Line" or "the Ottawa Valley Line".
2.	A pricing mechanism to provide sufficient incentives for the development of oil resources.
3.	Measures to ensure that any escalation in returns and revenues as a result of any higher prices will be used in a manner conducive to security and self-sufficiency.
4.	The early completion of a pipeline of adequate capacity to serve Montreal and, as required, more eastern points.
Mr. Speaker, the federal government recently announced the extension of the pipeline between Sarnia and Montreal, the construction of a second pipeline on Canadian soil, namely between Winnipeg and Montreal.
In January 1974, Parliament passed the emergency legislation on energy supplies.
As far as prices are concerned, consumers east of the Ottawa Valley Line have to pay a little more for their oil products. But following the Energy Conference held in Ottawa on January 22nd and 23rd at which the Federal government and the provinces agreed to hold a voluntary temporary price freeze on oil coming from Saskatchewan and Alberta, assurances were secured that the Federal government would protect the five Eastern provinces which have to rely on off-shore oil against the substantial increases they would have to face after February 1st, 1974.
The Federal government then agreed to maintain the price differential and assured Eastern residents that their prices would not increase on February 1st and that at the end of the voluntary freeze period in two months time prices would be even across the country, with allowances for freight costs. Then the Federal government will make substantial grants available to Eastern provinces so that costly off-shore oil will fall back to the same price as cheaper Western oil. The Federal government has resumed its talks with the oil producing provinces with a view to
The Address-Mr. Clermont
reaching by March 31, 1974 a consensus that will benefit all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, on August 3, 1973, the Federal government announced a new feed grains policy to be implemented in two stages. The first would be a concrete program for 1973-74 dealing with price parity between Eastern and Western Canada, and adequate supplies during the winter months. With respect to supplies, due to various circumstances, feed stocks in the province of Quebec in this period are far from being adequate, and I seriously wonder if groups and organizations would not be interested in seeing that program fail. We know that when that program was announced there were rather violent reactions to such a project. I urge the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) as well as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to make sure of that.
In another sector of agriculture, the Canadian Federation of milk producers has submitted to the federal government a series of requests to ensure these producers the incomes required to supply Canadian consumers with the dairy products they need, and a fair return for their work, their investments and their management skills. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the cabinet will seriously consider these requests and that the Minister of Agriculture, when he announces the government dairy policy for 1974-75, will also announce a substantial increase for industrial milk producers.
In going through the main estimates for the fiscal year ending on March 31, 1975, I note, in the estimates of the National Capital Commission, that an amount of $8 million will be spent on phase 2 of the highway network development in the national capital area north of the Ottawa river, that a further amount of $3,500,000 will be spent on sewers and $500,000 on public transportation.
The first two amounts are part of the comprehensive plan that the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada and the Minister of Transport had announced in 1969 and which will be carried out across the Ottawa river in the next 25 years.
As you remember, a general agreement on the improvement of the highway network on the Quebec side of the national capital area was reached on January 7, 1972, between the province of Quebec and the federal government, listing several projects to be carried out over a few years, such as the building of a bridge over the Gatineau river, the widening of Greber Blvd. from Maloney Blvd. in Gatineau to Archambault Blvd. in Gatineau Point, and the development of a limited access expressway from highway 8 in a south-west direction to the Gatineau river, as well as expressway A50 from Aylmer to Masson.
Mr. Speaker, I urge the parties who are negotiating the construction of this highway between the bridge on the Gatineau River, presently known as the "Pont des Dra-veurs", and Highway A5, to get this project under way soon so that the people living east of Pointe-Gatineau who have to go to Hull and Ottawa can use it and relieve the traffic on Greber Boulevard at peak hours.
Regarding the $500,000 contribution for public transport, it is to be linked with the agreement reached last fall between different government levels and agencies to

March 5, 1974
The Address-Miss MacDonald eliminate the traditional double fare applicable between Ottawa and Hull.
For many years now, the members of Parliament representing the Quebec part of the Ottawa region have asked for this measure, which has now taken the form of a $500,000 contribution from the National Capital Commission, made in the name of the federal government. The fact that there is now a transport commission on both sides of the Ottawa River probably helped to reach such an agreement.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the throne speech which we are now debating is conspicuous more for what it does not say than for what it does. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has described it as a matter of fact document. This is synonymous with saying that it is prosaic, ponderous, pretentious; in fact, dull. It lacks imagination, compassion, identifiable objectives. It is, however, a true reflection of the government which presented it-stolid, complacent, selfsatisfied, even sanctimonious; much like the Pharisee who looked at others in their misery and thanked God that he was not as they. That attitude on the part of the Liberals opposite, Mr. Speaker, is the cause of much of the malaise in this country today.
We are saddled with a government that lacks daring, innovation, imagination; a government that lags along day after day in the same old rut, lacking the will to fight the problems that beset millions of Canadians, afraid to depart from the well-worn practices of a bygone era and come up with some contemporary policies; a government that was old the day it was born.
It makes parliament watchers wonder whatever happened to such spirited individuals as Walter Gordon, Judy LaMarsh and Joe Greene with their free-wheeling ideas- individuals whom the Liberal Party used to encourage. One is left with the distinct impression that cabinet solidarity today means thinking alike, acting alike, doing nothing to upset the uniformity and sameness which characterizes this government.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Canadians today are beset by fears of inflation and the spiralling cost of living. For thousands upon thousands on fixed incomes, their weekly shopping is an agony to be endured as the purchasing power of their dollar goes steadily downward. There is no relief in sight, certainly not in this throne speech, for the escalating costs of bread, milk, sugar, meat-the staples; no relief in sight for the thousands of would-be home owners for whom the cost of purchasing a house is prohibitive. Nothing in this speech indicates that the government is concerned with preven-

tive health plans. Instead, the government adds to the worries of millions of Canadians by reducing the rate of funding available to the Medical Research Council from a 5.4 per cent annual increase to 2.5 per cent for 1974-75.
Under Liberal management, the prolonged scientific and medical struggle to combat cancer, heart disease, multiple sclerosis, genetic defects-all diseases-is downgraded. Senior medical researchers are being denied the funding they so grievously require. Some of our most talented scientists will be forced to leave Canada to continue their research in countries whose governments place a much higher premium on health protection. It is a sad commentary on the Liberal government that it sees fit to spend $100 per capita on unemployment insurance, but a mere $2 per capita on medical research. It is ludicrous to think that this government can spend $2 billion annually for unemployment insurance and only $40 million next year for medical research. Surely Canadians have a right and a duty to demand that government priorities and spending are brought into line with reality.
Mr. Speaker, reference to Canada's native peoples is almost non-existent in this throne speech. This cannot be attributed merely to the oversight of one minister but, rather, to the collective decision of an entire cabinet. Brief reference is made to rural and native housing programs. We shall have to await legislation for details, but I trust these programs will apply to native housing both on and off the reserves. Over 80 per cent of current native housing is substandard, and the rate of housing starts for native people has been running at half the rate of that for other Canadians. I trust the new legislation is designed to eliminate both these inequities and to eliminate the hardships in settlements such as Fort Rae, where 1,000 natives live in small wooden homes at temperatures sometimes of 60 degrees to 70 degrees below zero, homes heated primarily by wood stoves, homes without running water and indoor facilities. And there are many native communities such as Fort Rae across Canada.
There is nothing in the throne speech to indicate that the government is prepared to recognize and accept the principle of aboriginal rights; nothing to show that a native communications policy which will provide for continuing dialogue in their own languages is in the offing; nothing to indicate that the government is willing to meet its commitment to provide funding to Indian organizations so that the Indian Act can be revised by and for Indians, both male and female. I trust the minister will be making positive statements in all these areas in the near future.
The throne speech does make specific mention of guaranteed loans and other forms of assistance to both farmers and fishermen to assist them in purchasing or modernizing their equipment; incentives to increase Canada's catch of unexploited stocks of fish; and assistance to young farmers to provide sufficient financial incentives for them to establish themselves in farming. We will insist that these programs will apply, without question, to native people both on and off reserves and that the government will not try to fob-off requests from Indian bands for assistance under these new proposals by referring them to the ill-conceived, poorly administered, highly restrictive

economic development loan fund which they now have to cope with.
The native people, Mr. Speaker, get very short shrift in the throne speech. But that is becoming more and more a characteristic of this Liberal government. A senior civil servant, Walter Rudnicki, attempts to consult with the native council over housing policy and is summarily dismissed-not given the opportunity for discussion or even resignation, which we were told the other day is the "Liberal way", but cavalierly thrown out on his ear without notice. Why? Because of consulting with native people. That is short shrift indeed.
A few weeks ago the native people of the James Bay area were given very short shrift when the minister threatened to cut off legal aid in their battle to halt the massive James Bay project until their aboriginal claims are settled. Legal aid will be cut off, the minister says, if the Indians are "unreasonable". What does he mean by "unreasonable"? Surely, throughout this long-protracted struggle it is the minister himself who merits the description "unreasonable". He and his government have consistently refused to assume their constitutional and moral responsibility with regard to the James Bay native people. Rather, they have maintained a narrow, legalistic, rigid approach, lacking compassion, sensitivity and understanding.
During the recess the minister found it convenient to throw around terms like "unreasonable", while at the same time lavishing praise on the Bourassa government's handling of the situation. I hope that now these aberrations are past, he will assume the responsibility he has hitherto ignored and lend his full support and the weight of the federal government to backing the position of the native people of J ames Bay.
As I have said, the native people received only minimal reference in the throne speech, but that vast area north of the sixtieth parallel, two-fifths of Canada, fared even worse. It did not merit a single word. I realize the government has signified its intent to introduce a bill to amend the Yukon Act and the Northwest Territories Act. This will, I trust, mean significant amendments, not just a political restructuring to allow for a fully elected council, an executive committee, the addition or more councillors or the separation of the role of Speaker and Commissioner, important as these are, but significant amendment which will indicate this government is finally prepared to do something to remove the stigma of colonialism which permeates the north; that it will untie the apron strings from Ottawa; that it will hand over to the territorial councils fiscal responsibility for those areas already administered by the territorial civil service-education, housing and local government.
Unless that step is taken, unless the federal government is prepared to concede some of its fiscal authority, all other proposals are merely a charade, a farce perpetrated against 60,000 northerners who deserve something better. As legislators we, any one of us, would be appalled to participate in a legislative process of dealing with appropriations where we had the right to ask questions but were denied the right to propose changes, additions or deletions.
The Address-Miss MacDonald
At the recent Northwest Territories Council sessions in Yellowknife, some of which I attended, the elected councillor from the eastern Arctic pointed out that there were some 200 children of school age in his area with severe hearing defects, but that no programs or special facilities were provided for them in the education estimates. Neither, I might add, is there anything done for them by the federal Department of Health and Welfare. Imagine the frustration of this councillor who could indeed raise what one cannot help but recognize as a serious health and educational problem, but who had no power to suggest that expenditures be reallocated to allow for special training of these handicapped children.
It is this kind of responsibility, Mr. Speaker, which northerners should be allowed to exercise. They are close to the problems; they can recommend legitimate action and they should be accorded the fiscal power to enforce it. In the true interest of northerners, and in a real effort to eradicate the last vestiges of colonialism in Canada, I hope the minister is seriously considering incorporating such legislation in the amendments he will be proposing to the territories' acts.
Health care of native people, particularly those living in isolated areas, is woefully inadequate. Study after study points up the fact that native people are not provided with a treatment and public health program comparable to that enjoyed by residents elsewhere in Canada. We had a sad illustration of that just recently with the death of a two-month old Indian child in Alberta. Nowhere is this inadequate treatment more apparent than in the isolated communities north of the sixtieth parallel. Doctors are few, and dentists almost non-existent. There are only seven dentists employed by the Department of National Health and Welfare, and a few in private practice, to serve a population of 60,000 scattered across 1.5 million square miles.
An official of the Department of National Health and Welfare used these words to describe dental health among native northerners: "The conditions of teeth among the people of the north can best be described as 'oral sewers', and this stands in strong contrast to the universally healthy state of teeth that was seen before the native people were introduced to the white man's diet." The Nutrition Canada national survey report released last November contained a number of references to nutritional problems among Canada's native people. It spoke of vitamin C deficiency, vitamin A deficiency and other dietary related illnesses; but it went on to say that the data collected for the Indians and Inuit have not yet been fully analysed and a special report on these groups would not be available until at least six months after the initial report and recommendations of last fall had been released. Is it any wonder that our native people are made to feel as second-class citizens when they are continually relegated to the tag end position, to the status of an appendix on governmental reports?
A recent report on mental helath in northern communities observes that, first of all, it is apparent that a number of myths entertained by both northerners and uninitiated southerners alike must be laid aside if we are to seriously grapple with the many problems confronting our northern citizens. One of these myths is that people indigenous to

March 5, 1974
The Address-Miss MacDonald the north are a simple, contented lot, accustomed to the rigors of the Arctic environment and satisfied as long as white intruders leave them and their ecology alone. At one time this may have been true. Today it is definitely false. This is not to say that the Indian and Eskimo peoples do not love "the land", nor that they are helpless and despairing in contending with the elements. Quite the contrary.
The report goes on to say that it would be absurd not to recognize the cultural disintegration and change in lifestyle amongst the indigenous population which is a direct result of the inroads made by the white man's culture. Both native culture and natural ecology have been disrupted and traditional hunting economics, whether inland or coastal, would no longer seem to be viable. Virtually no Arctic community can now be considered self-sustaining.
One serious consequence of cultural erosion has been a loss of traditional control by the community over the behaviour of its members. This disruption and the dominating influence of southern educational systems and technology in northern settlements has irrevocably altered northern society. Therefore, the report states, while this is not a comparative study in the strict sense, it seems safe to say that the people of the north, whether white, Indian, Metis or Eskimo, want and need the same kind and quality of facilities and services available to southern Canadians. One might go so far as to state that because of the severity of the climate, the relative isolation and the long, dark winters, the need for a full range of high quality services and public amenities is much more acute in the north. Unfortunately, such services are not available and this lack is felt by all northern residents. For the aged and economically depressed, the problems of northern living are further compounded. This study was funded by a grant from the Department of Manpower and Immigration. It sets forward the facts in a very straightforward manner.
I mention these health reports which are particularly directed to problems in the north-hearing defects, lack of dental facilities, nutritional deficiences, mental health hazards-to show that they exist and that concerned Canadians are aware they exist. But if the throne speech is a true reflection of the Liberal government's thinking- and I have no reason to doubt it-then I can only assume that the cabinet is not particularly concerned with these problems.
The throne speech makes special reference to transportation as a key factor in regional development. It goes on to say that steps will be taken to ensure that Canada's transportation capability supports the government's national goals and is safe and efficent. Those two words "sufficient" and "efficient" interest me. At the present time the government is engaged in building a multimillion dollar highway along the Mackenzie corridor, a highway that was begun as a political come-on without the benefit of adequate, or even any social and evironmental impact studies. Is that highway safe from environmental damage? Is it efficient? Well, compared with what? The costs of the highway have escalated wildly since it was announced in April of 1972. The environmental and social hazards are rapidly becoming apparent even without the studies having been done; and the highway, it appears, has few ardent advocates except for a cabinet clique.

The Canadian gas Arctic consortium have publicly stated a highway is not necessary to their developmental plans, if and when a pipeline is built. The native communities have voiced their opposition on a number of occasions. They regard the Mackenzie River itself as their traditional highway. Residents of far northern communities such as Inuvik see no advantage to driving at least 1,000 miles to Yellowknife so that they can board a plane to fly to other centres farther south. They would go by air in the first place: the people in the north "think air."
If the government is serious in developing a transportation policy that is safe and efficient and which will contribute to regional development throughout the north, why does it not admit that a better alternative might be to use the $300 million to $400 million which has been estimated as the cost of the Mackenzie Highway, to hard-surface and enlarge existing airstrips, build new ones in those communities which are still isolated and, most important, subsidize air travel and air transport throughout the north? Such a plan would benefit northerners from Frobisher Bay to Old Crow.
The $300 million which is being spent on the highway would subsidize air transport for years to come and would eliminate intolerable inequities in the present travel costs, inequities which set the rate structure at $110 for an air ticket from Edmonton to Toronto, an air distance of 1,700 miles, but which demands a payment of $150 from Edmonton to Inuvik, an air distance of 500 miles less, or 1,200 miles. Travel costs in southern Canada are 6 cents per mile; in northern Canada 12 cents per mile-double the rate This is just another example of discrimination against northern Canadians. This injustice could be eliminated by equalizing transportation costs in the north of Canada as well as elsewhere in the country.
If this country is to achieve its full potential, equal consideration must be given to all Canadians and to all regions. The native people and the northern territories deserve the recognition this throne speech has denied them.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as has occurred several times before, I would most sincerely like to compliment the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. I would also like to compliment my leader on what I feel was an effective and worth while amendment to the motion proposed by the hon. members on the government side.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
In my view, the time has come for this House to face some harsh realities. When I listened to the Speech from the Throne I was disturbed to hear the net content that was being suggested by the government with regard to any plans they might have for the curtailing or control of inflation in this country. I was more disturbed than ever when I listened to the rambling, disjointed speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) when he entered this debate. One conference which he made I would again like to quote for the record:
I draw a similar parallel to allude to the goings-on in the New Democratic Party. It has to do with an ocean liner but the parallel is a bit different. It has to do with seagulls. Because they were squawking
March 5, 1974

and making a lot of noise, they thought they were actually running the ship.
Like many other members of the House, I laughed when the Prime Minister made that comment. If he chose to compare the NDP with the scavenger bird, the seagull, and suggest that somehow they were catching refuse from a ship, that comparison presumably was his right to make. However, it suddenly dawned on me, if the NDP are only the seagulls following the ship, who in fact is running the ship? Up to this point I had assumed the NDP were running the ship, the government of this country. We now have the admission that while we do have a majority government with two caucuses, neither caucus is completely sure of which is actually running the ship.
Having listened to the current Speech from the Throne and the speech of the Prime Minister, I thought it would be interesting to see what was said in previous throne speeches and by this Prime Minister since he took office in April, 1968, concerning inflation. The reason I say that is you will recall, Mr. Speaker, having received in this House estimates for the fiscal year 1974-75 that are truly startling. It has already been pointed out that these estimates contemplate an expenditure of 20 per cent more than was spent in the previous year, based on the original estimates. Perhaps it puts the magnitude of the government's spending spree into perspective when we realize that by the end of 1975 the government will have spent, at the federal level, $120 billion. Give them one more year and they will have spent, since they took office in 1968, more than has been spent by federal governments in Canada in the previous 100 years.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: These are the hard facts. Yet this is a government which when it took power in 1968 had the audacity to say it would control government expenditures.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What would you cut?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: We'll start with you.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is not only the growth of government spending which is startling; it is the growth in the monetary supply of the nation. In the past three years, for example, the money supply in Canada has increased by 53 per cent, an increase of 17 per cent per year on average. Government expenditure in the last six years has gone up faster than 20 per cent a year. Can anyone sensibly say that a government which induces such increases in our money supply and in federal spending is not an inflationary government?
Having mentioned this, I should like to refer to certain statements made in previous speeches from the throne. For example, on September 16, 1968, the speech said:
Parliament will be asked during the present session to consider proposals for a systematic and continuous review of prices and costs in our economy. Just as incomes cannot increase faster than productivity if price increases are to be restrained so government spending by all levels of government cannot increase faster than productivity if we wish to restrain the increase in levels of taxation. These two realities are among the most important that Canadians and their leaders much bear in mind during the months and years ahead.
The Address-Mr. Stevens
The speech went on to say that the government would be conscious of the limitations it must place on its expenditures. This is 1968, and bear in mind that inflation in that period was approximately one-third of the current inflation in this country. Speaking in the debate on the Speech from the Throne of that year, the Prime Minister said there must be "a freeze on civil service growth". He stated:
We have issued explicit guidelines to be used in the preparation of the estimates of 1969-70 and we shall not hesitate to take whatever other actions may be necessary to restrain the growth in our expenditures.
That was in September, 1968. I would draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker, that in the fiscal year ending March, 1968, total expenditures by the government of that time amounted to $9.9 billion. Today we are faced with an expenditure somewhat in excess of $23 billion, by the same government. Perhaps I might turn now to October 23, 1969, the date of the next Speech from the Throne. There it is stated:
In recent months the government has urged both the public and the private sectors to adopt special measures to combat the dangers of inflation. These measures, which the government has itself adopted, must be applied by all if further restraints are to avoided.
Again, speaking in the debate on that Speech from the Throne, the Prime Minister noted that the opposition parties had had much to say about the government's alleged failure to act in controlling spending. Mr. Speaker, there can be little doubt that history has shown the opposition parties were quite correct in their allegation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What about last year- wanting to double the estimates from your side?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I turn, now, to Hansard of October 8, 1970, where we find the following statement contained in the Speech from the Throne:
We are not yet free of inflationary pressure but there has been real progress and price increases have abated to the extent that the Canadian record in the battle against inflation is superior to that so far attained in any other western country. In the result it has been possible for the past several months to moderate certain monetary and fiscal restraints.
I would draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that the government then took credit for a better record than that of any other western industrialized nation. Yet today we are repeatedly told by the same government that there is little we can do about inflation in Canada, that we are caught up in the worldwide inflationary experience. I suggest the government is not being candid with the Canadian people. They know that inflation can be contained. They know what measures can be taken. But they hesitate, through lack of leadership, to take those measures.
Mr. Speaker, in the debate on the Speech from the Throne to which I have just referred, the Prime Minister made a startling comment. He said:
May I repeat at this point that the first step which was proposed to us was the fight against an inflation which had become a threat to the whole economy. Courage was needed to take that step.
Here we have a Prime Minister who said he felt he must take action against inflation, a threat to the whole economy. Yet the inflation to which he referred amounted, in fact, to one-third of the inflation we are presently

March 5, 1974
The Address-Mr. Stevens
experiencing. Is it unfair to assume that if there was a threat to the economy in 1970 or earlier, there is a triple threat today with inflation running at more than 9 per cent per annum?
Last session, Statistics Canada produced some very relevant figures which show how inflationary the present government has been in its first five years of office and in its latest year. Let me point out that during the St. Laurent government's five years in office ending January, 1958, inflation in this country amounted to 6.7 per cent. For five years of the Diefenbaker government ending in January, 1963, inflation was 7 per cent; in other words, 1.4 per cent on an annual basis. In the first five years of the Pearson government ending in January, 1968, inflation rose to 15.6 per cent. And in the first five years of the Trudeau government it went to 22.3 per cent. That was the most sensational five-year period of inflation Canada has had, barring wartime. In the past year, January, 1973, to January, 1974, inflation has increased another 9.1 per cent.
Is there no relationship between the government's spending as I have outlined it and the government's policy of printing money? Certainly the financial leaders of this country are becoming alarmed. For example, the largest life insurance company in Canada, Sun Life Assurance Company of Canada, through its president, Mr. Thomas Galt, stated at the annual meeting held on February 12 of this year:
It cannot be denied that the rapid growth in government expenditures and in the money supply in recent years have been major causes of the inflation we are having in Canada. Inflation must be combated-soon and effectively-or the damage to our economies, if not to our entire social order, will be irreparable.
That is what was said by the president of Sun Life, and I note that his words are very similar to the words of the Prime Minister in 1970 when he felt he had a better case to present than he has today. Mr. Earle McLaughlin, chairman and president of the Royal Bank of Canada, spoke to his shareholders on January 10 of this year and said:
I hope that the various governments would exercise restraint on the expenditure side, as a means to dampen inflation.
That was before the government tabled its $23 billion estimates for the current fiscal year. Surely there can be no suggestion that this is restraint. It is becoming customary for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), and I am pleased to see that he is with us tonight-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I never miss anything you say, and I never learn anything either.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That's because you're a slow learner.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is often said by the Minister of Finance and by his leaders, both on the New Democratic side and on the Liberal side, that somehow our inflationary record has been better than the inflationary record of the United States. In this respect, the Bank of Canada review of February, 1974, referring to the OECD report, puts the record straight, and I think it is time this government put the record straight concerning this comparison between the United States and Canada. In spite of virtually no inflationary pressure of the nature the United States has

had to live with, our record has been worse than the United States record in the past two years.
Let me quote from table 1 on page 6 of that Bank of Canada review. In 1972, United States inflation was 3.3 per cent, while ours was 4.8 per cent. In 1973, U.S. inflation-I emphasize that this is from a lower base-was 8.8 per cent, compared with our 9.1 per cent. Is it honest for the government to represent that somehow we have a better record than the United States? I suggest that such a statement is not correct. Not only has this government placed severe hardships on many people as a result of its inflationary handling of our economy; it has made millionaires of some individuals and corporations in this country.
I have already referred to the growth in our money system. You will recall that it is proposed in the throne speech that there be an amendment to the Bank Act. I will be very interested to see what the Liberal government intends to do in 1974 with respect to the banks, compared with what it did for the banks in 1967, the year of the great sell-out to the Canadian banks. I make reference to the fact that in that year banking legislation in this country was liberalized to such an extent that between 1967 and 1973 the banks were able to increase their earnings from $116 million to $321 million; that is the amount available for payment to their shareholders or for dividends. There are certainly some individuals and corporations who have truly prospered under the Trudeau government's rule, but I can assure you that it is not the poor man to whom the Prime Minister referred in his speech in this debate.
When explaining the government's record to Canadians, I believe it should be pointed out that when this government took power in April, 1968, Canadians paid $5.2 billion in income tax and in 1974 they will be required to pay twice that amount. This is before one even considers contributions to the unemployment insurance account which will add approximately another $1 billion to their tax load. It took 100 years from confederation to 1967 before the federal government's personal income tax levy reached $5.2 billion. Under the Trudeau government it took only six years to double that figure. That is the true impact of this high spending, high flying government which has the nerve to say that this House should continue to have confidence in it. It is time the people of Canada were asked who should run Canada.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: David Lewis.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Based on the estimates that have been tabled, after allowing for indexing-an idea that this government accepted from this party, and thank goodness- and after allowing for inflation, personal income taxes are likely to increase by more than 25 per cent as a result of this government's spending spree. If this forecast is borne out by the facts, this will mean that the increase in federal income taxes paid by Canadians will be $2.5 billion, or $200 million more than the entire tax paid by all Canadian citizens in 1963, the last year of the Diefenbaker government.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

March 5, 1974

and put all questions necessary to dispose of the amendment now before the House.
The question is on the amendment. Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the amendment? All those in favour of the amendment will please say yea.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yea.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
In my opinion the nays have it.
And more than five members having risen:

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Call in the members.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

I declare the amendment lost. This House stands adjourned until tomorrow at two o'clock.
